**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares; *left* and *right* mean the
offense's left and right. Q is the quarterback and R the running back; in flexbone pictures B is the
B-back (the fullback) and A an A-back (a slotback), W a wide receiver. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the
linemen. Defensive linemen are labelled by technique number, and S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will
linebackers. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks, thick dark arrows are ball carriers, and the
**dashed green line from the quarterback is his eyes**: the defender he is reading. Dashed arrows are a
play's *branches*: the paths the ball can take depending on the read. Receivers who do not matter to the
play are often left out of the box-sized pictures.

## The option principle: read one, block the rest

Start with the arithmetic you met in [03-01](03-01-run-game-language.qmd#why-a-quarterback-who-only-hands-off-leaves-you-a-man-short).
On a normal handoff, the quarterback gives the ball away and becomes a spectator. Nine offensive players
block or run routes, the ball carrier carries, and the defense has more defenders near the ball than the
offense has blockers. Some defender is always free. The only question is which one.

An [**option**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option) answers that question in the offense's favour. The
offense **chooses** the free defender in advance and leaves him unblocked on purpose. Then the quarterback,
holding the ball, watches what that defender does after the snap and hands the ball to whichever runner the
defender is *not* playing. The defender is not blocked, but he is not free either: whatever he does, he is
wrong. If he tackles the running back, the quarterback has the ball. If he takes the quarterback, the
running back has it. The read did the work of a blocker, and the blocker the offense saved is now blocking
someone else.

That is the whole idea, and everything else in this chapter is detail. Option coaches say it in one line:
**you don't block him, you read him.** The defender the quarterback watches is the
[**read key**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-key) (also called the
[**read defender**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-defender)).

### Which defender gets read?

Usually the [**end man on the line of scrimmage**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-end-man-on-the-line-of-scrimmage):
the outermost defensive player lined up on the line on one side of the formation. Coaches shorten it to
[**EMOLOS**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-emolos) or [**EMOL**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-emol),
and you will see both in coaching material. "On the line" means within about a yard of the ball, in a
lineman's stance or standing up; a linebacker four yards deep is *off* the line and doesn't count, however
far outside he stands.

Why him? Because he is the cheapest defender to leave alone. He is at the edge of the formation, so a
blocker would have to travel to reach him; he is usually a big, fast pass rusher who is hard to block
anyway; and on most runs he is the man whose job is to chase the play from behind or to squeeze it from
outside. If the offense can make his decision for him, the five linemen can spend their blocks inside, where
the double teams are.

```{python}
#| label: fig-emolos
#| fig-cap: "Finding the end man on the line of scrimmage (ringed), shotgun with one tight end on the right. Left: the defense has four linemen and nobody else on the line. On the left, the side with no tight end, the 5-technique is the end man. On the right, the 5-technique is inside the tight end, so he is still the last defender on the line on that side; the Sam linebacker is outside him but four yards deep, off the line, so he does not count. Right: the defense walks the Sam up to the line outside the tight end. Now he is the end man on that side, and the 5-technique is not. The count changes with every alignment, which is why the quarterback (and you) must find the end man again before every snap."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
for ax, walked in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    off = gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),))
    dfn = front7()
    if walked:
        dfn = [q.moved(d=1.0, w=6.6) if q.key == "SAM" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    p.highlight("SAM" if walked else "PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.0, 9.5), window=(-7.0, 7.5), title=False)
    say(f, p, 3.0, -6.4, "end man\n(left)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
    if walked:
        say(f, p, 3.6, 6.6, "end man\n(right)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 5.6, 2.8, "the 5 is now\ninside him", fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        say(f, p, 2.7, 4.3, "end man\n(right)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 6.4, 6.6, "Sam: off the line,\ndoesn't count", fontsize=6.6)
    ax.set_title("Sam walked up: he's the end man" if walked else "Four on the line",
                 fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The end man is the *usual* read key, not the only one. Later in the chapter you will see plays that read a
defensive tackle (the midline), the play-side end instead of the backside one (the inverted veer), and two
defenders one after the other (the triple option). The principle is the same every time: pick a defender
the offense would struggle to block, and make his choice the wrong one.

### What the option costs

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Option football exists because **an offense that blocks every defender it can reach still leaves the
defense a free man, and the option turns that man into a non-factor without spending a blocker on him.**
It also attacks the defense where it is strongest: the best pass rushers usually line up on the edge, and
the option makes the best of them guess. The trade is real, though. The quarterback has to be a genuine
running threat, or the defender simply ignores him. He takes hits, often from big men, on plays where he
keeps the ball, and sometimes on plays where he doesn't. Every exchange between quarterback and back is a
chance to fumble. And because the defense decides who gets the ball, the offense cannot always put the ball
in its best player's hands.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, an option play is a button press: you decide when to pitch. In real football, **the
defense decides**. The quarterback's job is not to choose who gets the ball but to see, in a fraction of a
second, which choice the defender has already made, and to take the other one. Good option quarterbacks
talk about it this way: the defender tells them what to do. That is also why option plays are so hard to
call against: a defensive coordinator who guesses right on the read defender only changes *which* runner
gets the ball.
:::

## The mesh: deciding in half a second

On most read plays the quarterback and the running back meet just after the snap, the quarterback holding
the ball in the back's stomach while both move toward the line. That meeting is the **mesh** (or *mesh
point*). Don't confuse it with the passing concept called mesh, which you will meet in
[04-04](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd); same word, different thing.

The mesh is a **ride**, not a handoff. The quarterback puts the ball in the back's belly, the back closes
his arms softly over it, and the quarterback "rides" him for a step or two, with his eyes not on the back
but on the read key. At the end of the ride he either lets go (the **give**) or pulls the ball back out and
runs (the **keep**). Those are the quarterback's two answers on every read, and the vocabulary is simply
[**give / keep**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-give-keep) (coaches also say *pull* for the keep).

What is the quarterback looking for? Not where the defender *is*, but what he can do *next*:

- If the read key **can tackle the running back**, because he is crashing down the line toward the mesh
  or squeezing inside, the quarterback **keeps**. The defender has taken himself out of the quarterback's
  path.
- If the read key **can't tackle the running back**, because he stays wide, sits, or rushes upfield
  outside, the quarterback **gives**. The defender is in position to tackle the quarterback, so the
  quarterback is the wrong man to carry it.

Teams differ on which answer is the default. A **give read** says: hand it off unless the defender
clearly takes the back away. A **pull read** says the opposite. Most teams teach the give as the default,
because the running back is the designated ball carrier and a hesitant keep is the worst outcome of all:
a quarterback who isn't sure should give.

Why does the ride matter? Because the defender has to commit too. A read key who sees the handoff
immediately can stop, wait, and play whoever comes out with the ball. The ride hides the ball and buys
time: by the time the defender knows who has it, he is already moving toward one of them.

## The zone read

The first option play most NFL fans saw, and still the most common, is the
[**zone read**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-read). You already know its pieces from
[03-02](03-02-zone-running.qmd). The line blocks **inside zone** to one side, every lineman stepping
play-side and double-teaming to the linebackers. As in plain inside zone, the defender farthest from the
play on the backside, usually the backside end, is not on anyone's list. On plain inside zone he is a
problem the quarterback can only fake at. On the zone read, he is the read key.

The two branches play out like this.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-read
#| fig-cap: "The zone read, two branches of the same play (the line zones right; the quarterback reads the backside end, ringed in orange; the green ring follows the ball). Top, the end crashes: at the mesh he is already sliding down the line at the running back, so the quarterback keeps and runs where the end used to be, with nobody left on that side to tackle him. Bottom, the end stays home: he shuffles wide and keeps his eyes on the quarterback, so the quarterback gives, the back runs the inside-zone track, and the end is now a yard or more too wide to tackle him. Simulated in Big Data Bowl coordinates; the box only, receivers and deep safeties left out."
def zone_read_play(keep):
    off = gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),))
    p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # defenders first (blocks aim at where they end up)
    go_to(p, "BT", (1.3, -2.1), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.4, 0.9), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.4, 4.3), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.5, -0.9), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 2.4), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.7, 5.8), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    # inside zone right
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.2, -1.0), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.6, -1.5)])
    go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RG", (2.3, 2.1), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "Y", (2.4, 5.3), speed=2.6, via=[(0.0, 4.7)])
    # the mesh: the back rides across the quarterback's face
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.0, 0.6), "run", speed=3.5, delay=0.25, via=[(-4.3, -0.4)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.9, 0.3), "path", speed=0.5)
    if keep:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.5, -2.0), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.15)
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.1, -0.4), "path", speed=2.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (3.0, 2.8), "run", speed=6.5, via=[(-1.2, 2.3)])
        go_to(p, "QB", (6.5, -7.0), "run", speed=6.8, delay=0.2,
              via=[(-4.6, -1.0), (-3.4, -3.6), (-1.0, -6.1)])
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-0.9, -5.6), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.15, via=[(0.4, -4.5)])
        p.handoff("RB", t=0.85)
        go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, 2.9), "run", speed=6.8, via=[(-1.2, 2.3)])
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, -4.1), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.2, via=[(-4.6, -1.4)])
    return p


TIMES_ZR = [0.0, 0.85, 2.4]
NOTES_ZR = ["Q catches the snap and\nlooks at the end", "End crashes at the back:\nQ pulls the ball", "Q runs where the\nend used to be",
            "Same snap, same look", "End stays wide:\nQ gives", "Back on the zone track;\nthe end is too wide"]
option_animation([zone_read_play(True), zone_read_play(False)], TIMES_ZR, lateral=(-10.5, 8.0),
                 window=(-6.8, 7.8), notes=NOTES_ZR, rows=["End crashes: keep", "End stays: give"],
                 rings=(("BE", style.DEFENSE),))
```

**If the end crashes** (top row of @fig-zone-read), he has done exactly what he would do against plain
inside zone: chase the running back from behind, down the line. Against a handoff, that is the play that
catches the cutback. Against the zone read, it leaves the whole backside empty. The quarterback pulls the
ball, the end tackles a back with no ball, and the quarterback runs around him.

**If the end stays home** (bottom row), he takes the quarterback away, so the quarterback gives. Now the
end is a step or two wider than he would have been on a normal run, which means the back's cutback lane,
the best part of inside zone, is wider too. Either way the offense got what it wanted from the one
defender it didn't block.

Count the hats to see why this matters. In the picture the defense has seven in the box (four linemen,
three linebackers) and the offense has six blockers (five linemen and the tight end). On a plain handoff,
that's one defender free, and inside zone picks the backside end to be him. On the zone read, the free man
is "blocked" by the read, and the box is seven against seven. Remember 03-01's lesson: the defense can
always bring one more defender than the offense can block, and the read is the offense's way of getting
that man back. Expect the defense to answer by bringing yet another one, usually a safety, which is the
[plus-one](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) idea that
[05-05](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) builds.

**What the zone read gives up.** The keep only gains *one* man. The quarterback who pulls the ball runs
into the next defender out: a linebacker flowing over the top, a slot defender, a safety coming down. If
nobody accounts for that man, the quarterback is running into a free tackler. That is why zone-read teams
add an [arc block](03-02-zone-running.qmd#tags-insert-arc-and-bash) (a tight end running past the read end
to block the next man) or a receiver block on the force defender, and why the quarterback has to be a
runner who can make that man miss. It is also why the quarterback is exposed: on every keep he is a ball
carrier in the open field, and on every give he can be hit while carrying out his fake, as you will see in
the rules section.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The quarterback decides whether to run." On a true read, he doesn't; the read key does. The quarterback's
skill is in seeing the decision early and riding the mesh long enough to make the defender commit. That is
why the best option quarterbacks are not always the fastest ones: a quarterback who reads the end cleanly and
keeps only when the end is truly gone gains more than a faster one who guesses.
:::

## The defense strikes back: the scrape exchange

If the offense reads one defender, the defense can answer by making that defender lie. The classic answer
is the [**scrape exchange**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scrape-exchange), which
[03-02](03-02-zone-running.qmd#tags-insert-arc-and-bash) previewed. The end crashes down hard on the
running back, every time, showing the quarterback a "keep" read. Meanwhile a linebacker who would normally
fill inside instead loops around behind the end (a **scrape**, in linebacker language: a sideways run
behind the line to a gap outside;
[05-04](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd) teaches it) to the
spot where the quarterback will be running. The end and the linebacker have *exchanged* jobs: the end takes
the back, the linebacker takes the quarterback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scrape-exchange
#| fig-cap: "The scrape exchange against the zone read (line zoning right; the quarterback reads the backside end). The end crashes inside at the running back, so the quarterback reads 'keep.' But the Will linebacker (ringed) was never going inside: at the snap he scrapes over the top of the end to the outside, and arrives where the quarterback is running. The read was right and the play still fails, because the defense swapped jobs between the two men the quarterback could see."
p = Play(gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)), front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "BE", (-2.4, -2.1), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "WILL", (-0.6, -6.1), "path", speed=5.5, via=[(3.4, -4.8), (1.2, -6.0)])
for k, end in [("LT", (0.4, -2.6)), ("C", (0.4, 0.5)), ("RT", (0.4, 3.7))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "LG", (3.2, -1.6), via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.8, -1.5)])
go_to(p, "RG", (3.4, 1.8), via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.8, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "Y", (3.2, 5.6), via=[(0.0, 4.7)])
go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 2.6), "run", via=[(-4.3, -0.4), (-3.6, 0.9)])
p.read("BE")
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-11.5, 8.0), window=(-7.0, 7.5), title=False, width_in=5.4)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.6, -1.1), (-3.3, -3.7), (-1.2, -5.7)], color=GREEN, label="keep",
       label_at=(-3.0, -6.6), fontsize=7)
tackle_x(f, p, -0.9, -6.4)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, -4.6), (-2.4, -2.1), "end crashes:\nQ reads 'keep'", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (5.7, -8.8), (3.4, -4.8), "Will scrapes over\nthe top to the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("The scrape exchange", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

The scrape exchange is clever because it beats the quarterback while he does everything right. He read
the end correctly; the end really could not tackle the quarterback. The defense simply put someone else
there. A cousin of the same idea, the **gap exchange**, has two defenders swap gaps after the snap in other
ways (a linebacker replacing a slanting lineman, for instance); it is built from the defense's side in
[Run Fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd), along with the other
ways a defense "fits" an option play.

The defense pays for the exchange, too. The scraping linebacker is no longer filling his gap inside, so the
give is now running at one fewer defender, and a running back who sees the crashing end can cut back into
the space the linebacker left. And a defense that exchanges every time is predictable, which is exactly what
the offense's counters feed on.

**The offense's replies** are the chapter in miniature, each one a different way of turning the
exchange against itself:

- **Bash** ([03-02](03-02-zone-running.qmd#tags-insert-arc-and-bash)): swap the runners. The back runs wide
  around the read end and the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside track. Now the crashing end has
  crashed onto the quarterback's fake and the scraping linebacker is chasing a back who started outside him.
- **Arc** ([03-02](03-02-zone-running.qmd#tags-insert-arc-and-bash)): send a tight end or H-back past the
  read end to block the scraper. The quarterback keeps into a lane with a blocker already in it.
- **Read someone else.** Leave the end blocked and read the linebacker instead, or read a defensive tackle
  (the midline, below). The defense's exchange only works if it knows who is being read.
- **Throw it.** If the linebacker is scraping outside at the snap, the space he left behind him is open for
  a quick pass. Packaging a throw with the read is the
  [run-pass option](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) (RPO), which gets its own chapter.

The defense, in turn, has answers to those. Option football is a conversation, and in 1960s Houston, 2000s
West Virginia and 2010s Baltimore it was usually the offense who spoke last.

## Inverted veer: the quarterback goes inside

The zone read sends the back inside and the quarterback outside. The
[**inverted veer**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-inverted-veer) (also called the
[**power read**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-power-read)) flips them: the **back goes outside** on a
sweep path, the **quarterback is the inside runner**, and the read is the **play-side** end, the defender
right where the play is going.

```{python}
#| label: fig-inverted-veer
#| fig-cap: "The inverted veer (power read) to the right. The line blocks power: the right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique with help from the right guard, who climbs to the Will; the center blocks back on the 1-technique; the left guard pulls through the hole for the Mike. The play-side end (ringed) is left unblocked and read. The back sweeps wide across the quarterback's face. If the end widens with the back, the quarterback keeps and runs inside him behind the pulling guard; if the end squeezes inside to take the quarterback, the quarterback gives and the back is outside him with the edge open."
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 0.6, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 4.0, 8.4, "NB")]
p = Play(gun(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 2.6), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])                 # down on the 3
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.2), via=[(-0.2, 1.9), (0.6, 1.4)])    # helps, then climbs to the Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))                                    # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.6), via=[(-0.6, -3.4)])               # hinge on the backside end
go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, 2.6), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.8, 1.4), (0.2, 3.4)])
p.read("PE")
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-7.5, 12.0), window=(-7.5, 7.5), title=False, width_in=5.6)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-4.7, 0.6), (-4.1, 4.6), (-1.6, 8.9), (3.0, 10.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="give if the end\nsqueezes", label_at=(-5.6, 9.6), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.8, 1.6), (-1.4, 3.2), (1.4, 3.3), (5.6, 3.3)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the end\nwidens", label_at=(6.0, 0.6), fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-2.4, -4.6), (-1.7, -1.2), "LG pulls", fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("Inverted veer (power read)", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

Why build it this way? Three reasons, each a trade.

**It puts the bigger runner inside.** Many running quarterbacks are big, strong men (Cam Newton, Jalen
Hurts, Josh Allen), better suited to running through a crease behind a pulling guard than to outrunning a
safety on the edge. The inverted veer gives them the inside track and a lead blocker: power blocking, with
the quarterback as the ball carrier.

**It attacks the edge with the back.** The running back, already moving sideways at full speed, gets the
ball going outside a defender who has just stepped inside. Defenses are taught to "squeeze" plays
inside-out with their end; the inverted veer makes that squeeze the wrong answer.

**It saves the blocker the play needed most.** On a power run to the right, somebody has to kick out the
play-side end, usually the fullback or a pulling guard (that is what the kick-out block in 03-03 is for).
The inverted veer doesn't block him at all. It reads him, so the pulling guard can go straight to a
linebacker instead.

What it gives up: the back is running sideways, not downhill, so if the read is wrong (the quarterback
gives when the end was actually wide), the back is running at a defender with no momentum and loses yards.
And the quarterback is a ball carrier between the tackles, in traffic, on every keep.

The name comes from the older **veer** (next section), in which the *back* is the inside runner and the
quarterback the outside one. Turn it inside out and you have the "inverted" version. Who invented the play
is unclear; it was made famous by TCU in 2009 and by Gus Malzahn's Auburn offense with Cam Newton in 2010,
when Newton won the Heisman Trophy and Auburn the national championship.[^iv]

## Speed option: straight at the edge

The fastest of the option plays, and the simplest to watch, is the
[**speed option**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-speed-option). There is no handoff and no mesh. The
quarterback takes the snap and runs straight at the end man on the line of scrimmage, with the running back
trailing him in **pitch relationship**: roughly four or five yards outside him and a yard or so deeper, so
that a toss can reach him without traveling forward. The end man has two runners coming at him. If he takes
the quarterback, the quarterback pitches; if he takes the back, the quarterback keeps and turns up inside
him.

```{python}
#| label: fig-speed-option
#| fig-cap: "Speed option to the right from the shotgun (the receivers on the left are out of the picture). The line reaches to the right and leaves the end man (ringed) unblocked; the slot receiver (H) blocks the nickel defender, the next man outside, from the inside out, and the Z blocks the cornerback. The quarterback attacks the end man's outside shoulder with the running back in pitch relationship. If the end takes the quarterback, the ball is pitched (dashed brown arc) and the back runs inside the slot's block; if the end widens to take the back, the quarterback keeps and turns up inside him."
off = gun(rb_w=1.6, extra=(O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z")))
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 0.6, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 10.0, "NB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RT", (3.8, 2.6), via=[(-0.3, 3.9), (0.9, 3.4)])      # skips the end, climbs to the Mike
go_to(p, "RG", (0.4, 2.9), via=[(-0.4, 2.2)])                  # reach the 3
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, 0.2), via=[(-0.4, 0.4)])
go_to(p, "LG", (0.4, -1.1), via=[(-0.4, -1.0)])
go_to(p, "LT", (3.6, -2.4), via=[(-0.4, -2.6)])
go_to(p, "H", (3.6, 9.4), via=[(1.0, 9.4)])                     # inside-out onto the nickel
go_to(p, "Z", (5.6, 16.0))
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.0, 4.6), "run", via=[(-4.4, 1.4)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.8, 8.0), "run", via=[(-5.6, 3.4), (-4.4, 6.6)])
p.read("PE")
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-6.5, 19.0), window=(-7.5, 8.5), title=False, width_in=5.8)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-2.0, 4.8), (-2.8, 7.8))
branch(f, p, [(-2.8, 8.0), (0.4, 7.6), (6.0, 7.4)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="pitch if the\nend takes Q",
       label_at=(-5.6, 10.2), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-2.0, 4.6), (0.6, 4.8), (5.4, 5.0)], color=GREEN, label="keep if the end\nwidens to the back",
       label_at=(6.8, 1.0), fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("Speed option", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

The speed option exists to get the ball to the edge **fast**, against a defense that is outnumbered there.
Count it in @fig-speed-option: on the right side the offense has the quarterback, the back and two blockers
(H and Z) against the end, the nickel and the cornerback. The end is read, the other two are blocked, and
the two runners face nobody until a linebacker or the safety arrives from inside. The play is over before
the defense can rally.

Its costs are the pitch and the quarterback. A **pitch** (the
[**pitch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pitch) is a one-handed underhand toss to the trailing back) has
to travel sideways or backward. A backward pass that hits the ground is a live ball, like a fumble, and
anyone can recover it; a toss that goes forward is legally a forward pass, and the offense gets only one of
those, from behind the line.[^pitch] So option teams drill the pitch endlessly, and a quarterback who pitches
under pressure, falling, with a defender hitting him, is the play's weak point. That is the other cost: on
the pitch branch, the end man has been *invited* to hit the quarterback, and he will, every time, often
just after the ball is gone.

## Veer and the triple option: two reads, three runners

Everything so far has had **two** possible ball carriers. The older option plays had **three**, and that is
where the modern idea came from.

The [**veer**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-veer) came from Bill Yeoman's University of Houston teams in
the mid-1960s. Yeoman had a weak offensive line that could not block a dive play straight up; his solution,
first used in the middle of a losing 1965 season that he expected to get him fired, was to stop blocking the
first defensive lineman outside the play-side tackle and read him instead.[^yeoman] The play-side tackle
releases inside to a linebacker, which makes the down lineman a free man, and the quarterback either gives
to a back diving just inside that defender or keeps the ball. A back trailing the quarterback adds a third
option. Yeoman's Houston teams ran it for two decades, and it spread across college football in the 1970s.

That three-way play is the [**triple option**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-triple-option), and it is
the play the [wishbone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wishbone) and the flexbone of
[02-03](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd) were built to run. It has three runners:

- the [**dive**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dive): the fullback (the flexbone's B-back) driving
  straight at the play-side guard's outside hip;
- the **quarterback**, who rides the dive, then, if he keeps, runs down the line toward the edge;
- the **pitch man**: an A-back who went in motion before the snap and is now trailing the quarterback in
  pitch relationship.

And it has **two read keys**. The first, the **dive key**, is the first defensive lineman on or outside
the play-side tackle; the second, the **pitch key**, is the next defender outside him, often an outside
linebacker or a safety who has come down. Everyone else is blocked.

```{python}
#| label: fig-triple-option
#| fig-cap: "The triple option from the flexbone, to the right, at the snap: the assignments. The backside A-back (A, left) has gone in motion and will be the pitch man. The B-back dives at the right guard's outside hip. The right tackle 'veer releases' inside to the Mike, leaving the 5-technique as the first read (the dive key, 1). The play-side A-back arcs around the next defender, the Sam standing on the line outside him, to the safety; that leaves the Sam unblocked as the second read (the pitch key, 2). The play-side receiver blocks the cornerback. Every defender on the right side is blocked or read."
def triple_play(react):
    off = flexbone()
    dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"),
           D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "3"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 8.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"),
           D("SS", "SS", 8.0, 9.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -2.0, "FS"),
           D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 12.6, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -12.6, "CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    check_legal(off)
    p.motion("LA", to=(-3.6, -1.6))                                   # pitch man in motion
    if react:   # this branch: the dive key squeezes the dive, the pitch key attacks the quarterback
        go_to(p, "PE", (-0.5, 2.7), "path", speed=3.8, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "SAM", (-0.6, 6.3), "path", speed=3.6, delay=0.55)
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.4, 2.4), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -1.2), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "SS", (5.6, 9.6), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "RCB", (5.4, 12.3), "path", speed=1.5, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "PT", (1.4, 0.9), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.6, 2.3), via=[(0.0, 2.6)], speed=3.0)            # veer release to the Mike
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 1.1), speed=1.6)                             # down on the 1
    go_to(p, "C", (2.2, -1.3), via=[(0.2, -0.4)], speed=2.5)           # climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -1.9), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -3.6), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RA", (4.8, 9.6), via=[(0.2, 7.0), (2.4, 9.2)], speed=5.0)  # arc to the safety
    go_to(p, "RW", (4.6, 12.4), speed=2.5)                             # block the corner
    go_to(p, "FB", (0.4, 2.6), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-2.6, 1.6)])     # the dive
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 1.0), "path", speed=3.0)                      # open to the mesh
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.5, 1.5), "path", speed=1.2)                      # ride
    if react:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-0.8, 5.9), "path", speed=5.5, via=[(-2.1, 3.5)])   # pull, attack the pitch key
        go_to(p, "LA", (6.0, 11.4), "run", speed=7.0, via=[(-4.3, 2.0), (-3.6, 6.5), (-2.0, 9.0)])
        p.pitch("LA", t=1.45)
    return p


p = triple_play(react=False)
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 15.0), window=(-6.5, 10.5), title=False, width_in=6.3)
read_line(f, p, (-2.5, 1.5), (1.0, 4.0))
read_line(f, p, (-2.5, 1.5), (1.0, 8.6))
branch(f, p, [(-3.6, -1.6), (-4.3, 2.0), (-3.7, 6.2), (-2.4, 8.8)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6)
say(f, p, 2.6, 4.2, "1", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8.5, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 2.6, 8.6, "2", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8.5, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 8.4, -6.6, "1 = dive key (first read)\n2 = pitch key (second read)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=7.0)
point_to(f, p, (-5.3, 4.2), (-2.4, 1.7), "dive", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (-5.2, -4.6), (-3.6, -1.6), "pitch man\n(in motion)", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-4.6, 10.6), (-2.6, 8.8), "pitch path", fontsize=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (8.6, 5.6), (2.4, 9.0), "A-back arcs\nto the safety", fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("Triple option from the flexbone", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

The quarterback's two decisions come one after the other, both in less than two seconds:

1. **At the mesh, read the dive key.** If he squeezes inside to tackle the dive, pull the ball. If he
   stays outside, or rushes upfield, give to the dive: it is going straight up the field just inside him.
2. **If he kept, run at the pitch key.** If the pitch key attacks the quarterback, pitch. If he widens to
   take the pitch man, keep and turn up inside him.

Here is one branch, in motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-triple-anim
#| fig-cap: "The triple option, one branch, in motion (simulated, Big Data Bowl coordinates; the green ring follows the ball). 1: the backside A-back's motion puts him behind the quarterback at the snap. 2: at the mesh the dive key (the 5, ringed) squeezes down on the B-back, so the quarterback pulls the ball. 3: the quarterback runs at the pitch key (the Sam, ringed); the Sam comes up to tackle him, so the quarterback pitches. 4: the A-back has the ball outside, with his teammates' blocks on the safety and cornerback in front of him."
option_animation([triple_play(react=True)], [-0.6, 0.85, 1.45, 2.3], lateral=(-8.0, 15.0), window=(-6.5, 10.0),
                 notes=["A-back in motion:\nthe pitch man", "Dive key squeezes the\ndive: Q pulls",
                        "Pitch key takes Q:\nQ pitches", "A-back outside the\nlast defender"],
                 rings=(("PE", style.DEFENSE), ("SAM", style.DEFENSE)), ncols=2)
```

The triple option is a machine for one thing: **making a defense play eleven men against eleven with every
assignment perfect, every snap.** Against it, a defense needs someone for the dive, someone for the
quarterback and someone for the pitch, on both sides of the formation, and it needs them to do their job and
nothing else. That idea, "assignment football," is how coaches describe defending it. A defender who does
two jobs (who tackles the dive *and* tries to get the quarterback) is doing neither. One player out of place
and the ball goes to the man he should have had.

Why isn't it everywhere, then? Because its costs are steep, and steeper the higher the level:

- **The quarterback takes a hit on nearly every play**, from the dive key on the pull and from the pitch key
  on the pitch. College option quarterbacks are built for that and are replaceable; NFL franchise
  quarterbacks are neither.
- **It needs under-center snaps and backs in the backfield**, which tilts the offense toward the run and
  makes passing harder (though option teams hit big play-action passes because the safeties have to play
  the run).
- **It is hard to come from behind with**: it runs clock and gains yards in chunks, not in bursts of
  passing.
- **NFL defenders are fast enough to cover mistakes.** A pitch key who is a step slow in college is a step
  fast in the NFL.

The triple option lives on where its trade still pays: at the service academies, in many high schools, and
for eleven seasons (2008–2018) at Georgia Tech under Paul Johnson, whose flexbone teams
[02-03](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd#the-flexbone) introduced. The full
college story, from the split-T to the wishbone to the spread option, is told in
[The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

## Midline: reading the man in the middle

The option doesn't have to read someone on the edge. The
[**midline option**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-midline-option) reads the **first defensive lineman
outside the center**, often a 3-technique, the defensive tackle on the guard's outside shoulder. The guard
in front of him leaves him alone and climbs to a linebacker. The dive back runs at the A gap, right at the
center's hip, and the quarterback reads the tackle.

```{python}
#| label: fig-midline
#| fig-cap: "The midline option from the flexbone, to the right. The 3-technique (ringed) is read: the right guard leaves him and climbs to the Mike, the right tackle blocks the end, and the center blocks back. The B-back dives at the A gap. If the 3-technique squeezes inside to tackle the dive, the quarterback keeps and runs just outside him, through the B gap; if he stays in his gap or rushes upfield, the quarterback gives and the B-back hits the A gap. The play-side A-back leads up on the Sam."
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 4.5, 5.8, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W")]
off = [q for q in flexbone() if q.key not in ("LW", "RW")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RG", (3.6, 1.6), via=[(0.3, 1.2)])                    # climb to the Mike
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 3.9))                                      # block the end
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.6))                                      # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, -2.4), via=[(0.3, -1.4)])
go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -3.6))
go_to(p, "RA", (3.8, 5.6), via=[(0.6, 4.4)])                    # lead up on the Sam
go_to(p, "LA", (-1.8, -2.4), "path")                            # fakes the pitch man's path
p.read("PT")
p.highlight("PT", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-8.5, 9.5), window=(-6.8, 9.5), title=False, width_in=5.4)
branch(f, p, [(-4.6, 0.0), (-2.6, 0.6), (0.4, 0.9), (6.2, 0.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="give if the 3\nstays put", label_at=(7.7, -1.4), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-1.9, 0.0), (-2.5, 0.6), (-1.0, 2.6), (1.2, 3.0), (6.2, 3.4)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the 3\nsqueezes", label_at=(7.7, 4.8), fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("Midline option", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

Why read a tackle? Two reasons. First, **the 3-technique is often the defense's best interior player**, a
penetrator who is very hard to block one-on-one (03-01 explains why the position became a star's job).
Leaving him unblocked and reading him neutralizes him the same way the zone read neutralizes an edge
rusher. Second, the midline **beats defenses that load up on the edge** to stop the outside options: if the
pitch and the keep outside are covered, the ball goes up the middle. Option teams use the midline as a
change-up when defenses crowd the edges: it reads a different man and attacks the middle.

The cost: the read is in the middle of the line, among bodies, with almost no time. A dive back in the A
gap is at the line in about a second, and a defensive tackle who reads the play can split the difference
(step inside and tackle the quarterback a step later). It is also a play of short gains by design; the
midline is a chain-mover, not a home-run play.

## Designed quarterback runs: adding a blocker

Everything above *reads* a defender. The other way to make the quarterback count in the run game is
simpler: **give him the ball on purpose.** On a designed quarterback run there is no read. The quarterback
is the ball carrier from the start, and that changes the arithmetic in the offense's favour, because the
**running back is free to block**. On a normal run, the back is the ball carrier and the quarterback
watches. On a quarterback run, the quarterback carries and the back blocks: the offense has gained a hat.

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-power
#| fig-cap: "QB power to the right, from the shotgun with one tight end (11 personnel; wide receivers out of the picture). It is the power play of 03-03 with the quarterback as the ball carrier: the tight end and right tackle block down, the right guard climbs, the center blocks back, the left guard pulls through the hole for the Mike, and the running back, freed from carrying the ball, kicks out the Sam on the edge. Seven defenders in the box (shaded) against seven blockers: a hat on every hat. On a handoff, the same front would leave one man free. The deep safety is out of the picture."
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W")]
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6, extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 4.2), via=[(-0.3, 4.6)])                  # down on the 5
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.6), via=[(-0.3, 3.0)])                 # down on the 3
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.6), via=[(-0.2, 1.8), (0.6, 1.0)])    # climbs to the backside Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))                                    # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.6), via=[(-0.6, -3.4)])               # hinge
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, 3.0), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.8, 2.0), (0.4, 4.6)])
go_to(p, "RB", (0.2, 5.8), via=[(-3.6, 3.8)], speed=5.0)       # kick out the Sam
go_to(p, "QB", (6.6, 5.2), "run", via=[(-4.6, 1.2), (-2.4, 3.8), (0.8, 5.0)])
p.highlight("RB")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-8.5, 10.0), window=(-8.0, 9.5), title=False, width_in=5.4)
x0, y0 = _P(f, p, 6.0, -5.2)
x1, y1 = _P(f, p, 0.0, 7.6)
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
f.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=GREEN, alpha=0.07,
                         ec=GREEN, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))
say(f, p, 7.4, -5.6, "7 in the box\nv 7 blockers", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-6.4, 7.6), (-3.6, 3.6), "R: now a blocker", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-3.6, -5.6), (-1.7, -1.2), "LG pulls", fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("QB power: the back becomes a blocker", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK,
               fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

There are four designed quarterback runs you will see most weeks.

- [**QB power**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-power) (@fig-qb-power): the power play, with the
  backside guard pulling through the hole and the running back as a lead or kick-out blocker. It is a
  short-yardage and red-zone favourite, because on third-and-2 the extra hat is worth more than anything a
  running back can do with the ball.
- [**QB counter**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-counter): the quarterback steps one way, as if
  running with the back's flow, then follows two linemen pulling the other way: one kicks out the end, the
  other leads through the hole (03-03's counter blocking). The back often runs the opposite way as a decoy
  or blocks the backside end the pulling tackle left.
- [**QB draw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-draw): a run disguised as a pass. The line shows pass
  protection, the quarterback shows a drop, and only when the pass rushers have charged upfield and the
  linebackers have turned to cover receivers does he run up the middle, through the space they left. It is
  strongest against man coverage, where defenders have their backs to the quarterback.
- [**QB sweep**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-sweep): the quarterback runs wide, with pulling
  linemen or the back leading him around the edge. It is the outside version of QB power, built for a
  quarterback with a running back's speed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-counter-draw
#| fig-cap: "Two more designed quarterback runs, both to the right side of the formation. Left, QB counter: the back, lined up on the left, blocks the backside end the pulling tackle left; the quarterback takes a step left with him, then follows the left guard, who kicks out the play-side end, and the left tackle, who wraps through the hole onto the Mike. Right, QB draw: the line sets as if to pass, the four rushers charge upfield, the linebackers drop to cover; then the quarterback runs up the middle, where they used to be."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
dl = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
      D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5")]
lbs = [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W")]
# counter
p = Play(gun(rb_w=-1.6), dl + lbs, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.6), via=[(-0.3, 3.0)])
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.4), via=[(-0.2, 1.8), (0.6, 1.0)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))
go_to(p, "LG", (0.1, 3.3), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.9, 2.4)])          # kick out the end
go_to(p, "LT", (3.8, 2.6), "pull", via=[(-1.8, -3.0), (-2.2, 2.2), (0.4, 3.6)])  # wrap to the Mike
go_to(p, "RB", (0.1, -3.7), via=[(-4.4, -3.0), (-1.6, -3.9)], speed=5.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (6.0, 4.4), "run", via=[(-5.4, -0.7), (-4.4, 0.9), (-1.4, 3.6), (1.0, 4.2)])
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-8.0, 9.0), window=(-8.5, 7.5), title=False)
say(f, p, -7.0, -2.6, "Q: step left,\nthen back right", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-5.6, 6.8), (0.1, 3.4), "LG kicks\nout the end", fontsize=6.6)
axes[0].set_title("QB counter", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
# draw
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6), dl + lbs, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, rush in [("PE", (-3.6, 5.6)), ("PT", (-2.0, 3.2)), ("BT", (-2.0, -2.6)), ("BE", (-3.6, -5.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, rush, "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "MIKE", (6.2, 3.6), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (6.2, -3.8), "path")
for k, w in [("LT", -4.6), ("LG", -2.0), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 2.0), ("RT", 4.6)]:
    go_to(p, k, (-2.3, w))
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, 6.0), "path", via=[(-4.0, 3.6)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.5, 0.0), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-8.0, 9.0), window=(-8.5, 7.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-6.5, 0.0), (-4.8, 0.2), (-1.0, 0.6), (5.6, 0.8)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="then run",
       label_at=(6.1, -1.0), fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -6.9, -3.6, "Q shows\na drop", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 3.4, 6.8, "LBs drop\nto cover", fontsize=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("QB draw", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The simplest designed quarterback run of all is the sneak, where the quarterback follows his center for a
yard; its pushed-from-behind version, the tush push, has its own story in
[Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Designed quarterback runs exist because **a quarterback carrying the ball turns the running back into an
eleventh blocker**, which no handoff can do. On short yardage and near the goal line, where the defense
crowds the box and every inch is contested, that extra hat is often the difference. The cost is the
quarterback's body: he takes the hits a running back takes, on purpose, and NFL teams pay their
quarterbacks too much to do that twenty times a game. So designed quarterback runs are a spice, used when
the extra blocker matters most and rationed the rest of the time.
:::

## How defenses answer the option

You have met the scrape exchange. Defenses have four broader answers, and you will see all of them on a
Sunday when an option team is in town.

**Assignment football.** Every option has a fixed number of ball carriers, and the defense assigns one
defender to each: someone for the dive (or the back), someone for the quarterback, someone for the pitch.
The rule is discipline. The defender assigned to the quarterback takes the quarterback even when the ball
was given, every time, and trusts that his teammate has the back.

**Make the read hard.** The read key does not have to commit. A defensive end can **slow-play** or
**feather** the read: shuffle down the line with his shoulders square, inside enough to threaten the back
and outside enough to threaten the quarterback, giving the quarterback a muddy picture until the last
instant. A slow-playing end wants the quarterback to give, so the defense can tackle the back with the
linebackers inside, or to hesitate, which kills the play.

**Out-number it.** Every option gains one man. The defense can bring one more into the box, usually by
rolling a safety down, and get its plus-one back. That is the box-count chess match of
[05-05](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd), and it is why option
offenses work best when the passing game keeps the safeties deep.

**Hit the quarterback.** The bluntest answer is also legal. Since 2013, NFL officials have treated a
quarterback who is carrying out a read-option fake as a runner: as the league's head of officiating, Dean
Blandino, put it, "the quarterback can be hit like a runner until he's clearly out of the play."[^hit] A
defense facing a read offense will tell its read key to hit the quarterback whenever he can, ball or no
ball, to make every keep, and every fake, cost something.

## Where option came from, briefly

Option football is older than the forward pass's dominance, and almost all of it was invented in college,
by coaches who had worse players than their opponents and needed arithmetic to win.

- **The split-T option, 1941.** Missouri's Don Faurot widened the T-formation's line splits and built a
  series of plays (a dive, a quarterback keep and a "running pitchout") that together worked like the
  modern option. Bud Wilkinson learned it from Faurot in the Navy during the war and took it to Oklahoma,
  whose split-T teams won a record 47 straight games from 1953 to 1957.[^faurot]
- **The veer, 1965**, Bill Yeoman at Houston, as above, and **the wishbone, 1968**, Emory Bellard at Texas
  ([02-03](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd#the-wishbone)): the triple option's
  two great formations.
- **The zone read, early 1990s.** At Glenville State, a small college in West Virginia, Rich Rodriguez's
  quarterback Jed Drenning bobbled a snap on an inside-zone play in practice in 1991, saw the backside end
  crashing, and ran where the end had been. Rodriguez saw that the mistake was a play.[^rr] He took it to
  Tulane and West Virginia, and Urban Meyer's spread-option offenses at Utah and Florida made it national.
- **The pistol, 2005**, Chris Ault at Nevada ([02-02](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd#pistol)):
  shotgun depth for the quarterback's read, with the back directly behind him so the run can go either
  way. In 2009 Ault's Nevada became the first team in major college football with three 1,000-yard rushers in
  one season; one of them was the quarterback, Colin Kaepernick.[^nevada]

The whole lineage, from the single wing through the spread option and the RPO, is in
[The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

## The NFL's on-and-off romance with option

For most of NFL history, option football was a college thing. Professional quarterbacks were pocket
passers, too valuable to be hit, and professional defenders were fast enough to punish a slow read. There
were exceptions, like Michael Vick's Falcons, and there were workarounds, like the 2008 Dolphins'
[wildcat](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd), which snapped the ball
directly to a running back to get the option's arithmetic without putting the quarterback at risk. But no
NFL team built its run game on the read until 2012.

**The 2012 wave.** In one season, four young, fast quarterbacks, three of them from college spread-option or pistol offenses, arrived
in, or took over, NFL offenses at once: Robert Griffin III in Washington, Russell Wilson in Seattle, Colin
Kaepernick in San Francisco and, a year after his own rookie season, Cam Newton in Carolina. Washington's
coaches, Mike Shanahan and his son Kyle, the offensive coordinator, married their outside-zone run game to
Griffin's pistol zone read, and the result was the league's top rushing attack: the rookie running back
Alfred Morris ran for 1,613 yards and Griffin for 815, then a record for a rookie quarterback.[^was2012]
In the playoffs, Kaepernick ran for 181 yards against Green Bay, a playoff record for a quarterback, mostly
on read plays the Packers seemed unprepared for.[^kaep] The season is remembered as the
[read-option wave](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd).

**The fade.** Then it cooled. Griffin hurt his knee in the playoffs that January and was never the same
player.<!-- VERIFY: Griffin's knee injury (torn ACL and LCL) in the Jan. 6, 2013 wild-card game against Seattle, and that it ended his breakout. -->
Defenses spent the 2013 offseason studying the read, the scrape exchange and the slow-play became
standard, and the league told officials that read quarterbacks could be hit as runners. Most coaches
concluded that the read option was a good change-up and a dangerous base offense, and through the mid-2010s
it became a few plays a game.

**The return.** Lamar Jackson changed the conversation. In 2019 Baltimore built an entire offense around his
reads, from the pistol and the gun, with zone read, inverted veer, speed option and designed quarterback runs,
and set the NFL's team rushing record while Jackson ran for 1,206 yards, a quarterback record, and won the
MVP award unanimously.[^ravens] Jalen Hurts's Eagles leaned on QB power, the read and the sneak; in Super Bowl
LVII he ran for 70 yards and three touchdowns, both Super Bowl records for a quarterback.[^hurts] Josh Allen
made the designed run a weapon for a pocket passer, especially near the goal line, and in 2024 the
Commanders' rookie Jayden Daniels broke Griffin's rookie rushing record.[^daniels] The Ravens era is the
subject of its own case study, [12-05](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd).

### What the numbers say

Can we see that history in data? Partly. The NFL's play-by-play does not record the play call, so it cannot
tell a zone read from inside zone. But it records **who carried the ball**, and it separately flags
quarterback *scrambles*, the unplanned runs when a pass play breaks down. A quarterback run that is not a
scramble, not a kneel-down and not a botched snap is, almost always, a **designed** quarterback run: a keep
on a read, or a planned quarterback run. We also set aside likely sneaks (up the middle, two yards or less
to go), because they are their own play with their own story. What is left is a fair proxy for the
quarterback run game this chapter is about.

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-run-data
#| fig-cap: "Designed quarterback runs in the NFL, regular seasons 2006–2025. Left: how often teams ran them, per team per game; the 2012 read-option wave is visible, then a plateau, then a second, larger rise from 2018. Right: efficiency, EPA per play, against running back carries in the same seasons. Designed quarterback runs are counted as runs by a player who threw at least 10 passes that season (so a gadget passer such as Taysom Hill counts), excluding scrambles, kneel-downs, aborted snaps and likely sneaks (middle runs with two yards or less to go). Read the right panel with the caveats in the text: the comparison is not like for like. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy."
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

style.apply()
SEASONS = list(range(2006, 2026))
cols = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "play_type", "epa", "success", "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel", "down",
        "ydstogo", "rusher_player_id", "rusher_player_name", "run_location", "game_id", "aborted_play",
        "passer_player_id", "pass_attempt", "yards_gained"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
reg = plays[plays["season_type"] == "REG"]
att = reg[reg["pass_attempt"] == 1].groupby(["season", "passer_player_id"]).size()
passers = set(att[att >= 10].index)
runs = reg[(reg["play_type"] == "run") & (reg["qb_kneel"] == 0) & (reg["aborted_play"] == 0)
           & reg["down"].notna() & reg["epa"].notna()].copy()
runs["qb"] = [(s, i) in passers for s, i in zip(runs["season"], runs["rusher_player_id"])]
runs["sneak"] = runs["qb"] & (runs["ydstogo"] <= 2) & (runs["run_location"] == "middle")
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(SEASONS).to_pandas()
backs = set(rosters.loc[rosters["position"].isin(["RB", "FB"]), "gsis_id"].dropna())
runs["kind"] = np.select([runs["qb"] & (runs["qb_scramble"] == 1), runs["sneak"], runs["qb"],
                          runs["rusher_player_id"].isin(backs)],
                         ["scramble", "sneak", "designed", "rb"], "other")
team_games = runs.groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique() * 2
des = runs[runs["kind"] == "designed"]
rb = runs[runs["kind"] == "rb"]
per_game = des.groupby("season").size() / team_games
epa_des, epa_rb = des.groupby("season")["epa"].mean(), rb.groupby("season")["epa"].mean()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 3.3))
ax = axes[0]
ax.bar(per_game.index, per_game.values, color=[style.SERIES[0] if s in (2012, 2013) or s >= 2018 else "#9ec5f4"
                                                for s in per_game.index], width=0.75)
ax.set_title("Designed QB runs per team-game", fontsize=9.5)
ax.annotate("2012\nwave", (2012.5, per_game[2013] + 0.03), xytext=(2009.6, 1.15), fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7))
ax.annotate("Lamar Jackson\nstarts (2018)", (2018, per_game[2018] + 0.03), xytext=(2014.8, 1.38), fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7))
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.6)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax = axes[1]
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
for ser, name, col in [(epa_des, "Designed QB runs", style.SERIES[0]), (epa_rb, "RB carries", style.SERIES[1])]:
    ax.plot(ser.index, ser.values, color=col, lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label=name)
    ax.annotate(name, (ser.index[-1], ser.values[-1]), xytext=(4, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                fontsize=7.5, color=col, va="center")
ax.set_title("EPA per play", fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlim(2005.5, 2031)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 0.35)
for a in axes:
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
    a.set_xticks([2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, 2025])
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()

d_all, r_all = des["epa"].mean(), rb["epa"].mean()
d_sr, r_sr = des["success"].mean(), rb["success"].mean()
d_first = des.loc[des["down"] == 1, "epa"].mean(); r_first = rb.loc[rb["down"] == 1, "epa"].mean()
third_share_d = (des["down"] >= 3).mean(); third_share_r = (rb["down"] >= 3).mean()
was12 = des[(des["season"] == 2012) & (des["posteam"] == "WAS")]
lj19 = des[(des["season"] == 2019) & des["rusher_player_name"].eq("L.Jackson")]
bal_rb19 = rb[(rb["season"] == 2019) & (rb["posteam"] == "BAL")]["epa"].mean()
rb19 = rb[rb["season"] == 2019]["epa"].mean()
peak = int(per_game.idxmax())
```

Three things to read from @fig-qb-run-data.

**The history is there.** Designed quarterback runs nearly doubled from the late 2000s to 2012–2013, settled
back, and then rose again, much higher, from 2018, peaking in `{python} str(peak)` at
`{python} f"{per_game[peak]:.1f}"` per team per game. Notice how small these numbers are: about one designed
quarterback run a game for a typical team, even at the peak. (Washington in 2012 had
`{python} str(len(was12))` of them, more than four a game; Jackson alone had `{python} str(len(lj19))` in
2019.) Most of the option's effect on a game is invisible in these counts, because **the read's main product
is the give**, a running back carry that looks like any other in the data.

**Per play, designed quarterback runs look far better than running back carries.** Across the twenty
seasons they averaged `{python} f"{d_all:+.2f}"` EPA per play against `{python} f"{r_all:+.2f}"` for running
backs, and a `{python} f"{d_sr:.0%}"` success rate against `{python} f"{r_sr:.0%}"`. On first down, where
the situations are most comparable, the gap is smaller but still there (`{python} f"{d_first:+.2f}"` against
`{python} f"{r_first:+.2f}"`).

**But the comparison is not like for like, and the right panel cannot tell you to run your quarterback
more.** Three reasons:

- *Selection.* On a read play, the quarterback keeps precisely when the defense has taken the back away,
  that is, when the keep is the open option. The keeps in this data are the reads that came out in the
  quarterback's favour; the reads that said "give" are filed under the running back.
- *Situation.* `{python} f"{third_share_d:.0%}"` of designed quarterback runs come on third or fourth down,
  against `{python} f"{third_share_r:.0%}"` of running back carries, often against defenses spread out to stop
  a pass. A run that converts third-and-4 is worth a lot of EPA.
- *Survivorship.* The quarterbacks who run often are the ones who are good at it: Jackson, Allen, Hurts.
  A team without one cannot buy their numbers by calling the plays.

The fairest reading is the one coaches reached on their own: **a quarterback who is a real running threat
makes the whole run game better**, partly through his own carries and partly through the gives and the
defenders he occupies. Baltimore's running backs in 2019 averaged `{python} f"{bal_rb19:+.3f}"` EPA per
carry, against a league average of `{python} f"{rb19:+.3f}"` for running backs that season; this data cannot
prove the reads caused that, but it is what the arithmetic predicts.[^data]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Washington 2012"}
Washington's 2012 offense is the cleanest NFL example of the zone read as a *base* play, not a gadget. The
Shanahans ran their outside-zone system from the **pistol**, with Griffin about four yards deep and Morris
directly behind him, so the back could run zone either way and the quarterback could read either end. The
line's first step looked like outside zone every time; the backside end had to decide whether to chase
Morris or stay home for Griffin, and Griffin, a former college hurdler, was one of the fastest quarterbacks in the league.

**What to notice** on the broadcasts and the All-22 of that season: the backside end's first step. Ends
who chased gave up Griffin keeps around the edge; ends who stayed home left wide cutback lanes for Morris.
Watch, too, how often Griffin carried out his fake after a give, running toward the sideline without the
ball: that fake kept the end honest on the next play, and it was also where he took hits.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers, NFC divisional round, January 12, 2013"}
Kaepernick's 181 rushing yards against Green Bay, in his eighth NFL start, are the read option's most famous
day in the NFL. San Francisco won 45–31. The 49ers ran their read plays from the pistol and the
shotgun, and the Packers' edge defenders repeatedly crashed down on the running back, leaving Kaepernick the
edge.<!-- VERIFY: contemporary breakdowns describing Green Bay's ends crashing on the 49ers' read plays. -->

**What to notice:** the read key on Kaepernick's long keeps. A crashing end takes himself out of the play,
and the free safety is too deep to arrive in time. Then watch the next season's tape of the same teams: the
crash-and-scrape became standard, and the long keeps got rarer. That is the defense learning.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2019"}
The 2019 Ravens are the read game as a complete offense: zone read, bash, inverted veer, speed option,
QB power and the sneak, run from the pistol and the gun with tight ends and fullbacks as extra blockers.
Jackson's `{python} str(len(lj19))` designed runs that season (by this chapter's count) averaged
`{python} f"{lj19['epa'].mean():+.2f}"` EPA per play.

**What to notice:** how many Ravens runs had *two* threats in the backfield on every snap, and how often the
read key was a linebacker or a slot defender rather than the end. Baltimore read whoever the defense left
free.<!-- VERIFY: film breakdowns of 2019 Ravens reads keying linebackers or slot defenders, not only the end. --> The defense's best answer, by the end of the era, was to put more defenders in the box and hit Jackson
whenever he carried out a fake; the full story, including how the offense changed when Derrick Henry arrived
in 2024, is in the [Ravens case study](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: find the read key.** Option plays happen fast, so do the work before the snap.

*Before the snap*

- **Where is the quarterback, and where is the back?** Shotgun or pistol with a back beside or behind the
  quarterback is the read look. A back offset to one side usually runs to the *other* side on the zone
  read (crossing the quarterback's face), which makes the end on *his* side the read key.
- **Find the end man on the line of scrimmage on each side.** Count from the outside in: who is the last
  defender standing on the line? Recheck after every shift; a linebacker walking up changes the answer.
- **Is anyone left unblocked on purpose?** You can't know until the snap, but look for a tight end or H-back
  lined up to the side away from the line's likely flow: he may be the arc blocker, which means read.

*At the snap*

- **Watch the read key's first step, not the ball.** Crash or squeeze inside: predict *keep*. Sit, widen or
  rush upfield outside: predict *give*. Say it out loud before the ball comes out.
- **If the end crashes, find the linebacker behind him.** Is he scraping outside? Then the keep is running
  into a scrape exchange.

*After the play*

- On the replay, check your call. Did the quarterback do what the read key "told" him? If not, was it a
  mistake, or was the defender slow-playing?
- On designed runs, count the hats: if the running back is blocking and the quarterback carries, the offense
  added a blocker. Did the defense answer with a safety in the box?

For your prediction log ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)): on every read look,
write the read key's position and your prediction (G or K) from his first step; afterward, write what
happened.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1: the end who always crashes.** Second-and-7 in the second quarter. The offense has run the zone
read four times today, the running back aligned on the left and the line zoning right each time, and on all
four the defense's backside end has crashed hard down the line at the back. Twice the quarterback kept, and
both times the Will linebacker, who lines up over the left guard, met him for a short gain near the left
sideline. The offense lines up in the same look again. If it runs the plain zone read, who probably makes the
tackle on a keep, and what should the offense call instead?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: gun, 11 personnel (tight end on the right), the back offset left; even front with the backside end (ringed) and the Will linebacker over the left guard. Two deep safeties out of the picture."
p = Play(gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)), front7(), los=35, to_go=7,
         title="Drill 1: 2nd and 7, the same look again")
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-11.0, 9.5), window=(-7.5, 8.0), width_in=5.2)
say(f, p, 3.2, -7.2, "crashed\n4 of 4", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The Will.** This is a scrape exchange: the end crashes to take the back and the Will scrapes outside to
take the quarterback. The end's crash is a *lie* told to the quarterback, and a plain zone read believes it
every time. If the quarterback keeps again, the Will is waiting; if he gives, the back is running into a
crashing end and a box with one fewer gap filled (a fair fight, but not the big play the offense wants).

**Better calls** use the exchange against itself:

- **Bash**: the back runs wide to the left around the crashing end and the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the
  inside-zone track. The crashing end has crashed onto nobody, and the scraping Will is chasing a back who
  started outside him.
- **Arc**: bring the tight end across (or line an H-back up on the left) to run past the end and block the
  Will. Now the keep has a blocker in front of it.
- **Read the Will instead**: block the end and read the scraper, or throw behind him (an RPO, 04-06).

The general lesson: an option defense that does the same thing every time has stopped being an option
defense. A good play-caller counts the crashes, as you just did.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2: two keys.** A college game on Saturday. The flexbone offense runs the triple option to its right.
At the mesh, the dive key (the 5-technique) **stays outside**, rushing upfield past the tackle. The pitch key
(the Sam) **widens** with the A-back in motion. Who gets the ball, and where?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: flexbone triple option to the right, at the snap. The dive key (the 5) and the pitch key (the Sam) are ringed; the backside A-back is in motion to become the pitch man."
p = triple_play(react=False)
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.title = "Drill 2: triple option right"
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 15.0), window=(-6.5, 10.5), width_in=5.6)
say(f, p, 3.0, 4.6, "1", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 3.0, 8.6, "2", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The B-back, on the dive.** The first read decides it. The dive key stayed outside, so he cannot tackle
the dive: the quarterback gives at the mesh, and the B-back hits the B gap just inside the 5, with the
tackle's veer release clearing the Mike. The pitch key's choice never comes into play, because the
quarterback never got to him.

This is the triple option's most common result, and its whole point: by staying outside, the dive key
"defended" the quarterback and the pitch, and so gave the offense a fullback running downhill at a
linebacker who is already blocked. Option coaches love the dive for that reason. A team that gains four
yards on the dive every time it is given can run the triple all day, and the defense must squeeze the dive
key inside to stop it, which opens the keep and the pitch.

If the Sam's widening had been the first thing the quarterback saw (if the dive key had squeezed and he had
pulled), the answer would be "keep": the pitch key took the pitch man, so the quarterback turns up inside him.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3: third-and-2.** Third-and-2 at the opponent's 36, fourth quarter, tie game. The offense lines up in
the shotgun with one tight end and the running back beside a quarterback who has run for 600 yards this
season. The defense puts seven in the box and plays man coverage on the receivers, with one deep safety.
Count the hats: on a handoff, how many blockers against how many box defenders? Which kind of run would give
the offense a hat on every hat, and what is the defense's likely answer?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: third-and-2, gun 11 personnel with the back to the quarterback's right, against seven in the box (four linemen, the Sam on the line outside the tight end, Mike and Will) and one deep safety; the three receivers and their man-coverage defenders are outside the picture."
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6, extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)),
         [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
          D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
          D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
          D("FS", "FS", 12.0, 0.0, "FS")], los=64, to_go=2, title="Drill 3: 3rd and 2, opponent's 36")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-9.5, 10.0), window=(-7.5, 13.5), width_in=5.2)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**On a handoff, six blockers (five linemen and the tight end) against seven in the box**: one defender free,
and on third-and-2 one free defender is usually enough. Man coverage on the receivers means the defense has
taken them away; nobody in the box needs to worry about a short pass to them.

**A designed quarterback run gives a hat on every hat.** With the quarterback carrying, the running back
becomes the seventh blocker: on **QB power** (@fig-qb-power) the back kicks out the Sam, the guard pulls for
the Mike, and seven blockers meet seven defenders. A **QB draw** is attractive too: man-coverage defenders turn
their backs to chase receivers, so the middle empties, and a quarterback who has run for 600 yards is a
threat a defense must respect. (A sneak is the shortest version of the same idea, if the line to gain were a
yard or less.)

**The defense's answer** is to account for the quarterback: put a [spy](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd) on him (a defender, often a linebacker,
assigned to shadow the quarterback), or bring the deep safety down as an eighth man and live with no help
deep. Either choice gives something back to the passing game, which is exactly the trade the quarterback's
legs create.
:::

## Takeaways

- An **option** leaves one defender unblocked on purpose and reads him. Whatever he does, the ball goes to
  the runner he isn't playing, so the read does a blocker's work and the offense gets back the man a handoff
  leaves free.
- The usual **read key** is the **end man on the line of scrimmage**; find him before the snap, and predict
  **give** or **keep** from his first step: if he can tackle the back, keep; if he can't, give.
- The families differ by who runs where and who is read: the **zone read** (back inside, quarterback outside,
  read the backside end), the **inverted veer** (back outside, quarterback inside behind a puller, read the
  play-side end), the **speed option** (quarterback and pitch man at the edge), the **triple option** (dive,
  keep, pitch, with two reads) and the **midline** (read a defensive tackle).
- **Designed quarterback runs** (power, counter, draw, sweep) don't read anyone; they turn the running back
  into a blocker. Their price, like every option's, is hits on the quarterback.
- Defenses answer with assignment football, the **scrape exchange** and gap exchanges, slow-playing the
  read, an extra man in the box, and hitting the quarterback; offenses answer back with bash, arc, new read
  keys and RPOs.
- The NFL adopted the read in **2012**, cooled on it, and returned to it with **Jackson, Hurts and Allen**.
  Designed quarterback runs look efficient per play, but selection and situation inflate that; their real
  value is what they do to the defense on every other run.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to tracking data.** The two animations in this chapter are gridiron simulations written in
NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates, so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. Big Data Bowl
releases carry a run-concept label in some editions, but they do not flag the read itself, so finding real
read plays means looking for the signature in the tracking: a quarterback and back who stay together for
half a second after the snap, and an end left unblocked. The cell below shows the shape of that code; it
is not run here, because the course does not download the Big Data Bowl files.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real tracking data; not run)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=2022091100, play_id=55)   # pick a zone-read play from plays.csv
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.8, 1.6, 2.4])
```
:::

[^data]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`load_pbp`) and rosters (`load_rosters`),
    regular seasons 2006–2025. Designed quarterback runs: `play_type == "run"` by a player with 10 or more pass
    attempts that season, excluding `qb_scramble`, `qb_kneel`, `aborted_play` and likely sneaks (`run_location
    == "middle"` with `ydstogo <= 2`). Checked against FTN charting's `is_qb_sneak` flag for 2022–2025, the sneak
    rule catches about three in four charted sneaks and rarely mislabels other runs. Running back carries: rushers
    listed at RB or FB. Aborted snaps matter: about one in seven non-scramble quarterback "runs" in the raw data is
    a botched snap, and leaving them in drags the quarterback average far below zero.
